title: Moshan Liaoran
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: The talk highlights the importance of approaching life with an open and non-judgmental mind, letting go of preconceptions and expectations. This is illustrated through stories of three women who have practiced Zen for many years, including Moshan Lioran, a 9th-century Chinese nun who taught that true understanding comes from personal experience and practice, rather than forced comprehension. By embracing life as it presents itself, we can cultivate equanimity and mindfulness in the face of challenges, leading to a more compassionate and authentic approach to everyday life.

As is the case with many women ancestors, there's not much known about her.
She lived in China in the ninth century, which is considered the Golden Age of Zen.
Her date of birth is unknown.
Her date of death is listed as 895.
She was a contemporary of the well-known woman teacher, Iron Grindstone Liu, and also the male teachers, Linzhi, Dongshan, and Zhaozhou.

Her name Moshan means summit mountain.
Mo is summit and Shan is mountain.
As was the tradition, she took the name of the mountain that was nearest to the monastery where she practiced.
She was a disciple of Deyu, and there's a chapter about her in the official Zen transmission records, the record of the transmission of the lamp that was written in 1004 of the common era.
I would have loved to read that chapter, but I couldn't find it online, and it's a multi-volume series of books, and I wasn't going to buy those just to read this one chapter.
But she was the first nun to be portrayed in Zen writing as undergoing the same training that was usually reserved for male teachers.
She may have been the second woman to receive mind to mind transmission after one of Bodhidharma's disciples in the sixth century in China.
Beyond that basic outline, there's not very much known about her.

The only other thing I could find is an encounter that she had with the monk when she was the abbess of Mount Moshan, and it's written up in this book, *The hidden lamp stories from 25 centuries of awakened women*.
It's a really nice book for many of us are using this book to find out about our women ancestors.
It's a collection of koans and stories about women starting at the time of the Buddha all the way up and up to modern day America.
So women from India, women from China, women from Japan and other places and America.
Each story has a commentary on it by a contemporary woman teacher.
So a very good book I recommend.
The encounter I'm going to talk about is also written up in Andy Ferguson's book, *Zen's Chinese Heritage*.
It's also mentioned in a couple of magazine articles, one by John Dido Laurie and another by Bill Porter, who's also known as Red Pine.
I will read you the story that appears in the hidden lamp.
The monk Gwansi Chion was sent by his teacher, Master Linji, to meet Master Moshan Lioran, a powerful women teacher.
When he arrived at Mount Moshan where she taught, he refused to bow or take off his traveling hat.
He asked, "What is Moshan?"
Moshan replied, "The summit cannot be seen."
He then asked, "Who is the master of Mount Moshan?"
And she replied, "Without the form of a man or a woman."
He shouted, "Why doesn't she transform herself?"
And she replied, "She is not a wild fox spirit nor a ghost.
What would you have her become?"
So Gwansi bowed and took off his hat.
He became the gardener at her monastery and he stayed for three years.
So Gwansi came to Moshan's monastery at the recommendation of his teacher, Master Linji, and undoubtedly he had expectations about what he would find there.
He undoubtedly had things he wanted and things he didn't want.
Isn't that like all of us?

If you start a new job or you move to a new place or you start a class and you walk into class for the first time, we all have things that we want and things that we don't want and things that we're hoping for.
I'm sure he had doubts about having a woman teacher.
Refusing to bow and take off his traveling hat shows his hesitation.
I'm sure that Moshan had lots of experience dealing with attitudes like that.
But you can see how being attached to surface appearances and fixed on your expectations and hopes can block you from seeing what's actually in front of you.
The question, "What is Moshan?" is usually interpreted to mean "Who are you?" or "What is the truth?"
Her answer, "The summit cannot be seen," is often thought to mean you have to discover this for yourself through your own practice and your own experience.
Isn't that true that there are so many people who can tell you all kinds of things, but until you actually discover it for yourself, it really doesn't sink in?
It's a little bit like somebody telling you what a food tastes like.
Then when you actually eat it for yourself, it's a whole different experience, and then you know what they're talking about.
She rightfully points out that expressing the Dharma does not depend on form, and so no transformation of form is needed.
Discovering what is true is hindered by our prejudice and by our distinctions and our preferences.
Guangxi eventually sees her wisdom and bows and takes off his traveling hat.
Later, when he was teaching, after he'd finished his training, he said, "I received half a ladleful at Papa Linji's place and half a ladleful at Mama Moshan's place.
And since I took that drink, I have not been thirsty."
So he was able to appreciate and incorporate what he learned from both teachers.
Now, in the Hidden Lamp, the commentary on this koan is from Shinshu Roberts.
She's a contemporary Zen priest in the tradition of the San Francisco Zen Center.
She's a Dharma heir of Sojun Mel Weitsman, who was abbot of Berkeley Zen Center for 40 or 50 years.
She's the co-founder of the Ocean Gate Zen Center in Capitola, California.
She's also a writer about Dogen.
She's a Dogen scholar.
She wrote a book called *Being Time*, which is an interpretation of Dogen's writings about time.
For those of you who aren't familiar with Eihei Dogen, he was a twelfth century Japanese priest who did extensive amount of writing about Zen and practice and reality.
He's considered the founder of Soto Zen, in my opinion, very hard to understand.
But Shinshu Roberts does a very good job of writing about him.
One sentence that she said in this commentary really stood out for me.
Here it is: *Our job is to meet our life fully as it presents itself, not as we would like it to present itself.
Don't get caught by the container.
Let your life come to you and meet it with an open and curious mind.* Now, Guangxi could have used that advice before he got to her monastery.
But I think that this statement is as good example as any I've ever encountered about one of the essential purposes of Zen practice.
That is to see your life as it actually is.

It's a hard thing to do, and it's why we practice for years and why we meditate so regularly because it's so easy to get sidetracked with your thoughts and your preferences and your resistance and your fantasies about what's really going on.
It's really hard to see your life, just as it is, just as it presents itself.
That statement reminded me of a couple of other brief statements that a couple other women teachers have made, contemporary women teachers.

So I thought for the rest of my talk I would tell you about a couple of other contemporary women teachers and what they said that I found so useful and that I try to keep in mind in my day to day life.
The next statement is from Jetsuma Tenzin-Polman.
She was born in England in 1943.
One of these, I'd say amazing people, when she was eighteen, she decided she was a Buddhist, so she took a ship to India by herself to look for a teacher.

I think it's really interesting to either meet somebody like that or read about somebody like that, a young person who knows from a really early age this is what I want to do, and they go for it, and they just do it for their whole life.
I didn't have a clue about what I wanted to do with my life until I was in my thirties.
So I think it's pretty remarkable.

I think Tim might be like that because I think he, not someone who didn't know what he wanted, someone, I think he started practicing Zen when he was eighteen or twenty, and he's kept it going, just solid for forty years.
So that's pretty remarkable.
Anyway, she took the ship to India.
She eventually found a teacher in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and was eventually ordained as a nun.
Then she went to a monastery for six years, and she was the only nun among one hundred monks.
In writing about and talking about those years, she said that the monks were always kind and respectful.
There was never any mistreatment or sexual harassment.

But because she was a woman, she wasn't allowed to participate in a number of the events at the monastery, and the monks would always wish for her that she would be born a man in her next life so that she could fully participate in monastic life.
After her six years of the monastery with the blessing of her teacher, she spent twelve years living by herself in a remote cave in the Himalayas, just meditating.
I'm sure she had occasional contact with her teacher, but most of that time, twelve years by herself.
Then she eventually founded a nunnery in India, where she lives today in retirement.
She says something we should listen to because she really put the time in.
The statement that she made was in an article in Tricycle magazine several years ago, and she said, *It is an obstacle.
Call it an opportunity.
It is an opportunity.
Nothing is extraneous from the spiritual life.* This is very important to understand.
Everything we encounter in our life, every moment of our life, is an opportunity to practice.
The last person I'll talk about is one of my favorites, I would say.
Charlotte Jilko Beck.
She lived from 1917 to 2011, so ninety-four years.
She was a student of Mizumi Roshi from Zen Center Los Angeles.
She founded the Zen Center San Diego, and she also wrote two books that I've always appreciated.
One is called *Nothing Special*, and the other is *Everyday Zen*.
These books are full of examples about how to practice Zen in day-to-day life.
She's a real character.
Our founding teacher, Norman Fischer, who helped found Red Cedar, named his organization the Everyday Zen Foundation with Jilko Beck's permission and blessing.
The thing that she said that I so appreciate is this: there is one thing in life you can always rely on, life being as it is.
Life is always going to be the way it is, so why can't we rely on that fact?
Trust in things being as they are is the secret of life, but we don't want to hear that.
I think what she's saying here is don't waste time wishing reality was any different than it is, because it won't do any good.
Things are the way they are.

That doesn't mean that you can't try to fix problems or make things better, but it's recommending that we see things as they really are without resistance or denial as the best foundation for figuring out how to respond.
I wish that I could tell you that I always keep these statements in mind and I use them every day.
I actually think they're all pretty much saying the same thing: see life as it is, don't fight it, and then figure out how you're going to handle it.
I don't use these all the time, but these statements are not far away.

When I find myself getting stirred up about things being not the way I want them to be, which happens quite often, whether it's a little thing like the weather or some personal thing in my life or something political or some of the big problems in the world, I do remember these statements.

I can usually draw on them to help me turn towards whatever is happening to me with some equanimity and some space to figure out what's the best way to handle this instead of just falling into my old habits, which have not, they're still there.
The old habits are still there.
For example, in February, I got all my income tax stuff done.
I usually do that for both of us, gathering all the stuff that's accumulated over the year and then filling out the many-page form that our accountant gives us.

I took it down to the accountant's office, and I really don't like doing my taxes, but I feel very good about getting them done and getting them out of the house and handing them over to the accountant.
That's okay, out of my hands.
A week or two later, the accountant calls and said, "Come on down, you know, sign your forms and you can pick up your taxes."
So Carolyn and I went down there.
We usually get, last year we got a couple hundred dollar refund.
We paid a couple hundred bucks, but we try to plan it so it's not too much either way.
That's what I thought was going to happen this year.
But no, we ended up owing way, way more than I've ever had to pay before.
I couldn't believe it.
Just like, "What?"
I was just sure there was a mistake.
I wanted to see the accountant right away, like, "How could this possibly happen?"
Of course, the accountant was busy and I couldn't do it.
In fact, I have an appointment next week to see him.
I managed to stay calm and not get upset at the person who was helping us.
We paid the bill and took our taxes home.
I looked at him and I might have figured out what happened.
But Carolyn and I talked about, "Well, what are we going to do?"
And pretty quickly we decided, "Let's just take the money out of savings, write a check to the IRS, mail it and forget about it.
I'll talk to the accountant, find out what happened, but let's just do that."
That's what we decided.
And so that's what we did.
I've done a pretty good job of just letting that be.
Be grateful that we had the money in savings and mail the check and don't stress about it.
I think that's been a pretty good way to handle it.
In the past, I would have spent a fair amount of time convinced that there had been a mistake, either mine or the accountant's or the IRS.
Then I would have spent a fair amount of time thinking about what I would rather have done with that money besides writing a check to the IRS.
Then I would have spent time thinking about the corporations and people who don't pay their fair share of taxes.
I would have gone over those three things a number of times, and it wouldn't have changed anything except I would have been more unhappy and harder to be around, I'm sure.
It seems like this was a much better way to handle it.
I contribute that to practice and also the good advice these women teachers.
The other thing I would say that I think is a really important factor is a regular meditation practice.

Day after day, week after week, month after month, year after year, because at least for me, I'm much faster at noticing when I've gotten off track, when I'm doing something about a situation that's just making it worse.
So I can pull myself back from the brink a lot quicker than I used to be able to.
So a lot less suffering.
Anyway, that's what I wanted to say about Moshan Lioran and the contemporary women teachers that I have found so helpful.
And again, I'm just very grateful for this practice and the sangha and thank you for listening.
Now, are we going to do the vows at the very end or do we do now?
Do the vows at the very end or do we do now?
